title: The commit and its objects
dek: A git commit is five small zlib files, two rewrites of the index, six lock files and one rename. This first part of a three-part teardown traces one git add and one git commit through git v2.55.0, call by call, then follows the objects they write: how an object is named, where git looks for it, how packs store it as a backwards byte delta, and how fanout tables and bitmaps make finding and counting objects cheap.
byline: 23 October 2026 · Subject: git@e9019fca (v2.55.0) · Part 1 of 3 · Read from the source and the manual; measured on this machine
description: Git v2.55.0 taken apart, part 1: one traced commit, loose object bytes and names, the object lookup chain, pack deltas, .idx fanout lookup, and reachability bitmaps, with measured numbers.
og_description: Part 1 of a three-part git teardown at v2.55.0 (e9019fca): one git add plus git commit traced call by call (five loose objects, six locks, one publishing rename, zero fsyncs), then the object header and hash, the lookup chain across sources, packs with backwards OFS deltas and a copy/insert codec, the .idx fanout lookup, and bitmaps that cut git.git's object count from 9.3 s to 0.14 s.
twitter_description: Git v2.55.0 taken apart, part 1: one commit traced call by call, then objects, packs, deltas, .idx lookup and bitmaps, with real bytes.

from the code marks a fact read from git at e9019fca (tag v2.55.0, 29 June 2026), cited as a path and line number from the repository root; the manual pages are cited under Documentation/. measured here marks a number, a byte dump or a behaviour observed with git version 2.55.0 on a 2-vCPU Linux box, either in a two-file lab repository with pinned dates (so every object id below is reproducible) or on a clone of git.git. Timings name their sample size; pack timings move by up to 40% between sessions, while byte counts and object counts are exact. reconstruction marks a judgement I drew from those sources rather than read in one place.

This is Part 1 of 3 of Git, taken apart. Part 2 covers the index, refs and the wire; Part 3 covers merging, maintenance and history, and ends with the findings register.
